title: Lecture 2 – Acromegaly, prolactinoma, pituitary tumours
html:
Source: CursII_MG-eng Oct 2022.pptx – 35 slides

LECTURE II #1

Topics: #2

  • Acromegaly and gigantism
  • HYPERPROLACTINEMIA
  • PITUITARY INSUFFICIENCY in adults and children

Acromegaly and gigantism Definition, Prevalence #3

  • GH-secreting pituitary adenomas are second in frequency to prolactinomas and cause the classic clinical syndromes of acromegaly and gigantism.
  • Prevalence: rare disease (3-4 cases/100.000)
  • = The characteristic clinical features are the consequence of chronic excessive GH and hence IGF-1 secretion. ;
  • the secretion of GH is autonomic, persistent and the GH’s dynamic control is abnormal
  • Overgrowth of bone is the classic feature, but GH excess causes a generalized systemic disorder with deleterious effects and an ↑ mortality rate, although deaths are rarely due to the space-occupying or destructive effects of pituitary adenoma.

Physiology of GH secretion #4

  • GHRH - SS
  • STH (GH)
  • Liver
  • IGF-I
  • Tissues
  • IGF-I
  • DIRECT
  • IGF-I-mediated
  • IGF-I = insulin-like growth factor
  • glycemia
  • (-)
  • (-)
  • :
  • Growth promoting
  • Metabolic effects: carbohydrate, lipid, phospo-calcic, hydroelectrolytic metabolisms
  • Most of the deleterious effects of chronic GH hypersecretion are caused by its stimulation of excessive amounts of IGF-1.
  • IGF-1= growth-promoting effects (DNA, RNA, and protein synthesis) → to the characteristic proliferation of bone, cartilage and soft tissues and ↑ in size of other organs
  • GH →insulin resistance and carbohydrate intolerance
  • GH has also direct effects on lipid, phospho-calcic, hydroelectrolytic metabolisms→
  • ⇒lipolysis, hypercalciuria, ↑ renal tubular reabsorption of phosphate , Na and water
  • GH and IGF-1 EFFECTS and pathophysiology of acromegaly
  • Pituitary GH is secreted under dual control of GHRH and somatostatin, and stimulates release of IGF-1 in the liver and elsewhere. IGF-1 has peripheral actions, including bone growth, and exerts negative feedback to the hypothalamus and pituitary

Clinical ad pathogenetical forms of GH excess #5

  • Clinical features of GH hypersecretion depend on the age at the onset of pathological lesion :
  • The onset of chronic GH excess in childhood and adolescence (! Prior fusion of the epiphyses)= GIGANTISM
  • ! Most of these patients have associated hypogonadism, which delays epiphysial closure, and the combination of IGF-1 excess and hypogonadism leads to a striking acceleration of linear growth. ( height > +3 SD for age and sex)
  • Tall stature!!!!

Clinical ad pathogenetical forms of GH excess #6

  • The onset Of GH hypersecretion in adulthood
  • (after the fusion of the epiphysis of long bones, linear growth does not occur )
  • = ACROMEGALY, the syndrome characterized by local overgrowth of bone, particularly of the skull and mandible

Etiology and Pathogenesis #7

  • 1. GH- SECRETING PITUITARY ADENOMA OR MIXT GH-PRL SECRETING PITUITARY ADENOMA - >95-99% of cases
  • GH –secreting pituitary adenoma (acromegaly) is the most common type of pituitary adenoma associated with a genetic abnormality.
  • Predisposing factors include mutations causing syndromic diseases or isolated pituitary adenomas (see Table below).
  • Several genetic syndromes are associated with pituitary tumors and GH hypersecretion
  • MEN type 1 (Multiple endocrine neoplasia) ( Wermer syndrome)
  • GH-secreting pituitary adenoma
  • Primary hyperparathyroidism
  • Pancreatic tumors ( gastrinomas, islet cell tumors..)
  • MEN type 4
  • McCune–Albright syndrome and
  • Carney complex ( a genetic disorder by multiple benign tumors most often affecting the heart: myxomas, skin and endocrine system and abnormalities in skin coloring (pigment) resulting in a spotty appearance to the skin of affected areas.)
  • Familial isolated pituitary adenomas (FIPA)
  • ← genetic defects in the aryl hydrocarbon receptor interacting protein (AIP) gene, which probably acts as a tumor suppressor.

Etiology and Pathogenesis #8

  • 2. PARANEOPLASTIC SECRETION OF GHRH-like/GH-like substances
  • Ectopic production of GH-releasing hormone (GHRH) leads to pituitary somatotroph hyperplasia.
  • carcinoids, pancreatic(islet) tumors, lung carcinoma, hypothalamic hamartoma are the most frequent sources of ectopic GHRH

Clinical features of acromegaly #9

  • ←the effects of excess GH/IGF-1,
  • ←excess PRL in some (as there is co-secretion of PRL in a minority (30%) of tumours) or, rarely, stalk compression), and
  • ←the tumour mass (space -occupying manifestations of the pituitary adenoma: hypopituitarism, visual field defects, headache)

The characteristic clinical manifestation= #10

  • ACROFACIAL DYSMORPHISM (DISFIGUREMENT)
  • A combination of bone and soft tissue overgrowth leads to a typical acromegalic facies
  • Photographs show a slow, insidious transformation of the facial features over several years

Acromegalic facies #11

  • Bone and cartilage changes affect chiefly the face and skull: thickening of the calvarium, ↑ size of the frontal sinuses→ proeminence of the supraorbital ridges and frontal bossing
  • enlargement of the nose; downward and forward growth of the mandible→ prognathism,
  • Patients may seek care for dental problems (teeth separation, malocclusion)

Slide 12 #12

  • The deformations affecting the spine results in dorsal kyphosis, which with deformation of rib cage, leads to the classical "punchinello" aspect
  • Soft tissue growth also contributes to the facial appearance, with coarsening of the features, deep nasolabial furrows and facial and infraorbital puffiness;
  • -macroglossia; large lips;
  • -sonorous deepening voice occurs in association with laryngeal hypertrophy and enlarged paranasal sinuses.

Slide 13 #13

  • The hands and the feet are predominantly affected by skeletal hypertrophy and soft tissue growth (98 to 100% of patients); they are large, thickened and bulky, with blunt, spade-like fingers and toes
  • → ↑ in ring, glove, hat and shoe size - patients routinely recall repeated resizing of rings and changes in shoe size (and hat size) (mostly widening).
  • SOFT TISSUE CHANGES:
  • thickening of the skin, with increased oilines and sweating;
  • acne, sebaceous cysts, and fibromata mollusca
  • ( skin tags and papillomas);
  • acanthosis nigricans of the axillae and neck;
  • hirsutism or hypertrichosis in women

ARTICULAR AND NEURAL MANIFESTATIONS #14

  • Acromegalic arthropathy can affect up to 84% of the cases
  • Bone and cartilage overgrowth → arthralgias and in long-standing cases to degenerative arthritis of the spine, hips and knees;
  • Neural enlargement and wrist tissue swelling →CARPAL TUNNEL SDR (← painful median nerve compression)→ acroparesthesias;
  • Proximal myopathy → myalgias, cramps
  • RESPIRTORY MANIFESTATION
  • Sleep apnea, both obstructive and central, is very common
  • - prognatism, thick lips, macroglossia, and hypertrophied nasopharyngeal structures may obstruct airways; tracheal intubation may be difficult;
  • both central respiratory depression and airway obstruction lead to paroxysmal daytime sleep ( narcolepsy), sleep apnea, and habitual excessive snoring

Clinical features #15

  • GH excess leads to generalized visceromegaly, evident as as thyromegaly and enlargement of the salivary glands. Enlargement of other organs—liver, heart, kidney is usually not clinically detectable.
  • Gastrointestinal features: constipation ← long and tortuous colon
  • The incidence of colonic polyps (and colonic carcinoma) appears to be increased
  • CARDIOVASCULAR MANIFESTATIONS
  • Hypertension-in 36-40 % of patients;
  • Left ventricular hypertrophy, valvulopathies and arrhythmias are also more prevalent in these populations.
  • → a complex cardiomyopathy characterized by concentric hypertrophy (predominantly affecting the left ventricle), diastolic dysfunction and progressive systolic impairment eventually leading to heart failure.
  • cardiac enlargement may be secondary to -hypertension
  • -atherosclerotic disease
  • -acromegalic cardiomyopathy

Other endocrine and metabolic abnormalities: #16

  • ENDOCRINE MANIFESTATIONS
  • Diffuse or nodular goiter
  • Galactorrhea/ gynecomastia (mixt adenoma)
  • Diabetes mellitus/IGT
  • Hypertriglyceridemia type IV, ↑Lp a;
  • Hypercalciuria
  • Nephrolithiasis (secondary to the hypercalciuria induced by GH excess)
  • +
  • Lethargy or fatigue
  • Weight gain
  • Hyperhidrosis
  • Heat intolerance

Investigations of acromegaly #17

  • A. LABORATORY (HORMONAL ) FINDINGS
  • Acromegaly is usually clinically obvious and can be readily confirmed by measurement of GH secretion; basal fasting GH levels are greater than 10 ng/ml in more than 90% of patients.
  • 1. GH-IGF-1 axis
  • GH – levels vary according to age (VN =1-5 ng/ml)
  • !however, single, random measurements are not entirely reliable (although normal healthy subjects have undetectable GH levels throughout the day), because GH secretion is episodic in acromegaly and because other conditions may ↑ GH secretion
  • Factors affecting GH secretion
  • ↑ – exercise, sleep, stress (physical or psychologic, ex. Venous puncture ), hypoglycemia
  • ↓ – postprandial hyperglycemia, elevated free fatty acids
  • Suppression with oral glucose is the simplest and most specific dynamic test for acromegaly
  • • Glucose suppression test – 75g oral glucose with GH determinations at 0, 30 and 60 minutes;
  • • Interpretation:
  • in healthy subjects oral administration of 75 g of glucose causes a reduction of the GH level to less than 1 ng/mL (<0.4 ng/ml with new ultra -sensitive assays) at 60 minutes;
  • in acromegaly there is failure to suppress GH to <0.4 ng/ml in response to a 75g oral glucose load and this lack of response establishes the diagnosis.
  • or, especially for diabetic patients, mean GH >1 ng/ml and IGF1 levels superior to upper limit of normal for age and sex.
  • IGF-I ( IGF-1 results must be interpreted according to the patient’s age and sex!)
  • 2. PRL (Serum PRL should be measured, as some tumours co-secrete both GH and PRL or cause pituitary stalk compression leading to functional hyperprolactinemia),
  • 3. Assessment of the anterior pituitary gland function( hypopituitarism?) FSH, LH, estradiol/testosterone, TSH/FT4, ACTH/cortisol

MRI/CT scan- of pituitary fossa #18

  • MRI (both before and after the gadolinium administration) is the current procedure of choice for imaging the hypothalamus and pituitary
  • →the tumour (98%) and whether there is extrasellar extension, either suprasellar or into the cavernous sinus.
  • B. IMAGISTIC STUDIES

Radiologic Signs SPECIFIC TO ACROMEGALY: #19

  • Thickening of the calvarium
  • Enlargement of the frontal and maxillary sinuses
  • Prognatism
  • Hypertrophy of the anterior clinoids= “acromegalic beak “
  • Lateral plain film of the skull
  • IMAGING STUDIES
  • Lateral plain films of the skull ( focused on the sella turcica)
  • sellar enlargement in 90% of cases +

Diagnosis #20

  • Radiographs of the hand:
  • ↑ soft tissue bulk
  • ‘’arrowhead ‘’ tufting of the distal phalanges
  • ↑ width of intra-articular cartilages
  • cystic changes of the carpal bone
  • Radiographs of the feet show similar changes and there is ↑ thickness of the heel pad (normal <22 mm)

Investigations of acromegaly #21

  • C. PERIMETRY (for VISUAL FIELD defects), VISUAL ACUITY when the tumor is found to abut the optic chiasm on an imaging study.
  • →bitemporal hemianopsia or unexplained visual field defects or visual loss
  • D.OTHERS (for associated comorbidities)
  • THYROID AND ABDOMINAL ULTRASONOGRAPHY (→VISCEROMEGALY)
  • COLONOSCOPY – polyps/ colon cancer
  • OTHERS
  • Calcium and phosphorus metabolism
  • ↑serum phosphorus,↑calciuria, ↑ AF
  • Carbohydrate metabolism – ITG (impaired glucose tolerance)/DM
  • ECG si ecocardiography - LVH/global, ventricular enlargement (cardiomegaly); allows evaluation for systolic (↓EF) or diastolic ventricular impairment (heart failure)

COMPLICATIONS #22

  • 1. cardio-vascular and cerebrovascular diseases
  • 2. sleep apnea
  • 2. Acromegalic arthropathy :progressive cosmetic deformity and disabling degenerative arthritis
  • 3. colonic cancer
  • 4. neurologic complications: carpal tunnel syndrome
  • 5. kidney stones

Treatment #23

  • Objectives:
  • to halt progression of the disorder and to prevent late complications and excess mortality
  • Removal or destruction of the pituitary tumor, reversal of GH hypersecretion and maintenance of normal anterior and posterior pituitary function
  • THERAPEUTICAL METHODS
  • Surgical treatment
  • transsfenoidal selective adenoma removal is the procedure of choice (primary therapy) in most patients
  • craniotomy is necessary in the rare patients in whom the major suprasellar and lateral extension precludes the transsphenoidal approach
  • ! Patients with persistent GH hypersecretion after surgery should receive medical treatment and/or radiotherapy.

Slide 24 #24

  • a) Somatostatin analogs (SST receptor ligands (SRLs): lead to suppression of GH secretion in 20–60% (up to 75%) of patients, decrease IGF-1; however, tumor reduction occurs in a much smaller percentage
  • Indications:
  • - the therapy of choice for those with residual GH hypersecretion following surgery
  • may be used as primary therapy for patients with macroadenoma > 2 cm or with whom the risks of surgery or anesthesia are unacceptable (for patients with severe pharyngeal thickness and sleep apnea, or high-output heart failure)
  • 1st generation of SRLs binds preferentially to somatostatin receptor (SSTR)-2):
  • Preparations include octreotide LAR and lanreotide acetate given by injection every 4 weeks
  • LANREOTIDE (SOMATULINE) 30mg /14 days im
  • LANREOTIDE Autogel® 90-120 mg/month deep sc
  • OCTREOTIDE LAR® (SANDOSTATIN LAR) 10, 20, 40 mg/month i.m.
  • Side effects of this class of agents consist mainly of gastrointestinal symptoms and the development of gallstones.
  • 2nd generation of SRLs binds to multiple SSTRs, with high affinity to SSTR subtype 5 in addition to 2,3, 1
  • PASIREOTIDE (Signifor LAR ®) im 40-60 mg/ 4 weeks
  • Treatment may increase the response rate in patients with acromegaly, but glucose tolerance declines and patients may develop diabetes mellitus (in addition to side effects that are similar to those of octreotide and lanreotide)
  • An oral preparation of octreotide has also been recently developed and has been currently tested.
  • 2. Medical treatment

b GH receptor antagonist #25

  • PEGVISOMANT(Somavert®)-for patients who failed therapy with surgery and SSTR ligands
  • 10-30-40 mg/daily sc
  • SE: liver toxicity
  • Monotherapy or combined with SSTR ligands of 1st or 2nd generation and/or cabergoline
  • Monitoring of liver biochemistry is necessary for safety
  • Serial imaging with MRI scan to evaluate tumor size in a patient receiving pegvisomant is also recommended.
  • c DOPA agonists
  • GH + PRL mixt tumors
  • GH-secreting pituitary tumor(are most likely to be useful in patients with just modest elevations of GH and IGF-1 levels, with or without concomitant hyperprolactinemia)
  • CABERGOLINE 2-4 mg/week
  • d. REPLACEMENT TREATMENT FOR HYPOPITUITARISM
  • (see pituitary failure)

. Radiotherapy –IIIrd/IVth line #26

  • → Radiation therapy should be reserved for those patients with residual tumor mass following surgery, and if medical therapy is unsuccessful, or not tolerated; in a patient who is uncontrolled after surgery and medical therapy (and not as primary therapy)
  • Radiotherapy (RT) - is generally considered as an adjuvant therapy
  • Major drawbacks:
  • -prolonged delay in achieving reduction in GH levels (GH levels may not return to normal until 10 to 15 years after therapy) and
  • -the appreciable incidence of hypopituitarism
  • gamma knife radiosurgery (preferred over CRT)-used for tumors confined to the sella (50-70% remission rate at 2 years following therapy is reported in some limited series);
  • fSRT

HYPERPROLACTINEMIA and PROLACTINOMAS #27

Etiology #28

  • PRL is secreted from the anterior pituitary and its release is inhibited by dopamine produced in the hypothalamus
  • PRL hypersecretion = the most common abnormality due to hypothalamic-pituitary disorder
  • Pathogenesis:
  • Pregnancy, hypothalamic-pituitary disorders, primary hypothyroidism, and drug ingestion are the most common causes.
  • During pregnancy, serum prolactin levels increase 10-fold, reaching levels of 150 to 300 µg/liter by the term.
  • !!!However, the most common cause of hyperprolactinemia is drug ingestion, and a careful history of drug intake must be obtained.

Slide 29 #29

Table 5. Causes of hyperprolactinemia
Physiologic: pregnancy, sucking, stress, sleep, exercise !!!Note that the stress of venipuncture may cause mild hyperprolactinemia
Pharmacologic (antipsychotic agents are the most likely to cause hyperprolactinemia) Dopamine receptor blockers (phenothiazine, haloperidol, metoclopramide), Neuroleptics: risperidone, chlorpromazine, Estrogens: estrogen therapy or oral contraceptive use H2 antihistamines: cimetidine, ranitidine, Pantoprazole Antidepressants: fluoxetine, amitriptyline, Labetalol, verapamil
Pathologic 1. Prolactinomas (PROLACTIN-SECRETING ADENOMAS) 2. Hypothalamic-pituitary stalk compression/ hypothalamic lesions→↓local dopamine levels (functional, “disinhibition hyperprolactinemia”): head trauma, suprasellar surgery, infiltrative diseases (e.g., sarcoidosis), craniopharyngioma, suprasellar pituitary mass extension. Hypothalamic lesions frequently cause PRL hypersecretion by decreasing the secretion of dopamine that tonically inhibits PRL release; similarly, a traumatic or surgical section of the pituitary stalk leads to hyperprolactinemia and hypopituitarism. Nonfunctional pituitary macroadenomas frequently cause mild hyperprolactinemia by compression of the pituitary stalk or hypothalamus. 3. Systemic diseases Primary hypothyroidism CRF (chronic renal failure) Severe liver disease PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome)

Clinical features #30

  • Are the same regardeless of its cause
  • In women
  • Galactorrhea : spontaneous/ induced , permanent/ intermittent
  • Menstrual disorders
  • primary/secondary amenorrhea
  • oligomenorrhea
  • Infertility; estrogen deficiency symptoms : ↓ vaginal lubrication, osteopenia, irritability
  • ↓ libido, weight gain, hirsutism
  • In men : the usual manifestations are those of hypogonadism
  • Erectile dysfunction
  • gynecomastia
  • galatorrhea – exceptional
  • infertility
  • ↓ libido= the initial symptom
  • Mass effects (macroadenomas only): headaches and visual field defects (uni- or bitemporal field defects), hypopituitarism, invasion of the cavernous sinus that may lead to cranial nerve palsies.

Investigations of prolactinomas #31

  • General evaluation
  • Basal PRL levels (2 determinations), gonadotropins; FSH, LH should be established (+ serum testosterone/E2 in ♂/♀).
  • Serum prolactin is assessed with the use of assays that yield accurate values, and assessment usually presents no challenges in the clinical setting. Assay-specific normal values are higher in women than in men and are generally lower than 25 µg/liter.
  • Free T4 and TSH levels, liver and kidney function should be assessed as well.
  • A pregnancy test should be performed in women with amenorrhea. (please see etiology of hyperprolactinemia)
  • Specific Diagnosis
  • When other causes of hyperprolactinemia have been excluded, the most likely cause of persistent hyperprolactinemia is a prolactinoma.
  • Note: There is a general correlation between the PRL elevation and the size of the pituitary adenoma →in the presence of a pituitary mass on MRI, the level of prolactin helps determine whether the mass is a prolactinoma or a non-functioning pituitary tumour causing stalk-disconnection hyperprolactinaemia:
  • with very rare exception, basal PRL levels greater than 200 to 300 ng/ml are virtually diagnostic of prolactinoma.
  • A prolactin level greater than 500 µg/liter is diagnostic of a macroprolactinoma whereas mild to moderate hyperprolactinemia (serum PRL >100 µg/liter and in particular greater than 250 µg/liter) is suggestive of a tumor, either a microprolactinoma or a non-functioning macroadenoma compressing the pituitary stalk.

Diagnosis #32

  • Imaging MRI of the pituitary
  • is necessary if there are any clinical features suggestive of a pituitary tumour, and desirable in all cases when prolactin is significantly elevated
  • ■ Microadenomas usually appear as hypointense lesions within the pituitary on T1-weighted. Stalk deviation or gland asymmetry may also suggest microadenoma.
  • ■ Macroadenomas are space-occupying tumors, often associated with bony erosion and/or cavernous sinus invasion.
  • Visual field assessment
  • Formal visual field testing is recommended when the tumor is found to abut the optic chiasm on an imaging study.

Treatment of prolactinomas #33

  • Aims of therapy:
  • ⇒ resolving hyperprolactinemic symptoms or reducing tumor size.
  • Microprolactinomas: restoration of gonadal function.
  • Although most microadenomas do not progress, treatment of these patients is recommended to restore normal estrogen levels and fertility and to prevent early osteoporosis secondary to persistent hypogonadism.
  • Macroprolactinomas: reduction in tumor size and prevention of tumor expansion and restoration of gonadal function.

Treatment of hyperPRL #34

  • Medical treatment = DOPAMINE AGONISTS
  • = The treatment of choice (in prolactinomas and “disinhibition” , functional, hyperPRL)
  • treatment leads to suppression of PRL in most patients, with subsequent normalization of gonadal function and termination of galactorrhoea. Tumor shrinkage occurs at a variable rate (from 24h to 6–12 months) and extent and must be carefully monitored.
  • CABERGOLINE (DOSTINEX®) 0,5 mg/tb, ½--2tb/day twice/week ( has a better side-effect profile; it is as effective as bromocriptine in ↓ macroadenoma size and is more effective in ↓ PRL levels)
  • BROMOCRIPTINE (BROCRIPTINA, PARLODEL®) 2,5 mg/tb; the dosage: 5-30 mg/day in divided doses
  • Quinagolide
  • SE: dizziness, postural hypotension, nausea, vomiting; cardiac valve disease (right-sided cardiac fibrosis) (echocardiographic evaluation ).
  • Surgical treatment
  • Medical therapy failure from drug intolerance or resistance
  • Pituitary apoplexy
  • Prophylactic- massive macroprolactinoma- before planned pregnancy
  • Radiotherapy- for patients with PRL-secreting macroadenomas who have persistent hyperPRL and who have not responded to attempts to control their pituitary adenomas with surgery and dopamine agonists/for rapidly growing tumors (→prevents further tumor expansion)
